source.title: Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds
source.authors: Eric J. Michaud; Liv Gorton; Tom McGrath

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how feature geometry, especially multidimensional manifolds, affects SAE latent allocation and scaling, using synthetic manifolds and decoder-geometry measurements rather than the original toy-superposition method.
record.gate_note: The study reports synthetic-manifold SAE scaling and measurements of decoder nearest-neighbor cosine similarity on real-model SAEs. It does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, neuron polysemanticity, or SAE feature recovery/completeness. Latent-frequency slopes are used to speculate about feature-frequency exponents, not as a direct test of the claim; cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes multidimensional feature manifolds exist and models how SAEs would allocate latents to them. Its results describe SAE behaviour on synthetic manifolds and decoder geometry of existing SAEs. None of this measures whether network features are superposed, whether they are 1-D or multi-dimensional, or whether SAE latents recover the model's units. The authors say they cannot tell whether real SAEs are in the pathological regime, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors present a capacity-allocation model in which SAEs over-tile common manifolds when beta < alpha, and say they cannot resolve whether real SAEs are in that regime. They call their most important observation that radial variation causes early plateaus and basis-like solutions. If that geometry is realistic, manifolds may not harm SAE scaling. They frame the work as posing the problem rather than answering it.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a capacity-allocation model and trains SAEs on synthetic feature manifolds, then measures decoder geometry on real-model SAEs; it does not reproduce the original toy-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The per-feature loss curve depends on manifold geometry: hollow hyperspheres can continue improving with many latents, whereas manifolds with radial variation plateau early.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE per-feature loss curves on synthetic manifolds depend on geometry. Hollow hyperspheres keep absorbing latents (beta ~0.05 up to 10^4 latents). Shells with radial variation plateau near 2d_i latents (basis solution), for both ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether SAEs over-tile a multi-dimensional feature manifold depends on the manifold's geometry (radial variation leads to early saturation).

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma Scope layer-12 SAE decoders show skewed but not extreme nearest-neighbour cosine similarity; the few >0.97 pairs have dead neighbours. An Inception-v1 SAE shows many very-high-similarity neighbours, possibly duplicates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real SAEs show little decoder-geometry evidence of massive manifold tiling in LLMs; vision SAEs differ.

record.problems: The authors state that they do not know the real feature-frequency distribution or the geometry of real feature manifolds, so they cannot determine whether the pathological regime occurs in practice. The real-model geometry results are qualitative and largely presented as plots; the high-similarity latents examined in one Gemma SAE had dead nearest neighbors, and the Inception result may reflect duplicated latents.
record.rows_left_out: The model-derived allocation equations and numerical simulation in Sections 2.5–2.6 were not recorded as experimental rows; they are model analysis rather than measurements of neural-network feature geometry. Other individual curves in Figures 3 and 6 are not separately listed because the text does not provide condition-specific numerical outcomes beyond the grouped results recorded above.

untested.parts: No toy network storing more sparse features than dimensions; no sparsity transition or geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition among features in a network. The allocation model concerns SAE latents, not neurons.
No measure of feature spread across neurons or of SAE recovery of known features in real models.
Argues SAE latents could tile manifolds instead of discovering rare features, but gives no measurement of completeness, stability or canonicity in real SAEs. Authors leave it unresolved.
Assumes multi-dimensional features (citing Engels et al.) but does not test whether real network features are 1-D or multi-dimensional.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's V6 'tested' status and limits_scope label removed: synthetic manifolds are imposed inputs to an SAE, not evidence about network feature dimensionality. Figure 4 latent-frequency slopes (-0.74 for 16k, -0.57 for 32k) are not rows; they are used only to speculate about alpha and bear on no version. Section 2.5-2.6 derivations and simulation are model analysis, correctly left out. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only to motivate the linear representation assumption.

versions.untested_parts: No test of sparse features competing in a small network with more features than dimensions, or of the claimed sparsity-dependent transition and regular superposition geometry.
The paper models allocation of SAE latents across features, but does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether important features get dedicated neuron dimensions while others share.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising from mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The paper does not measure feature spread across neurons or test whether an SAE recovers sparse features from real models.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
The synthetic experiments test how SAEs scale on multidimensional manifolds, but do not directly establish the dimensionality of features in real networks or test superposition itself.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured reconstruction-plus-sparsity loss while scaling the number of SAE latents on points on a circle.

conditions.value: L1 penalty; coefficient not stated here

rows.measure: Total SAE loss and manifold tiling by latents
rows.value: Figure only; text reports that loss can decrease gradually by tiling the circle with more sparsely activating latents, with dozens of latents accommodated before loss plateaus.
rows.note: The text describes the qualitative result but does not give numerical loss values.
rows.check: Measures SAE loss when an SAE reconstructs a hand-built circle. That is an SAE property, not a network's feature dimensionality (V6). Figure-only result.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.size_stated: At least 10^4 latents before loss plateaus for the reported higher-dimensional hyperspheres
rows.operation_detail: Measured the per-feature SAE loss curve as the number of latents increased.
rows.measure: Per-feature loss scaling and measured slope β
rows.value: The curves accommodate at least 10^4 latents without loss plateauing; measured β is roughly 0.05.
rows.note: The paper reports the dimension range and slope together; it does not give separate numerical slopes for dimensions 6, 7, and 8.
rows.check: SAE loss scaling on synthetic unit hyperspheres (beta ~0.05, dims 6-8). The manifolds are imposed by design, so this says nothing about whether real features are 1-D.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3 caption; Appendix A.1, discussion of beta; Figure 5 caption

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-feature loss curves as the number of latents increased.

conditions.value: spherical shells with radial variation, dimensions 2–9

rows.value: The loss curves plateau quickly; in the more realistic radial-variation setting, saturation occurs at approximately n_i ≈ 2d_i.
rows.note: The text describes this as a basis-like solution rather than continued manifold tiling.
rows.check: SAE saturation at about 2d_i latents on synthetic shells. This is about the SAE's learned solution, not network representations. 'Partial' has no version to be partial against.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3, right panel and caption; Appendix A.1, radial-variation discussion

rows.subject: JumpReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-feature loss curves as the number of latents increased.

conditions.value: spherical shells with radial variation, dimensions 2–9
tanh loss with c = 0.1 and λs = 1.0

rows.value: The curves plateau after allocating roughly 2d_i latents to the feature manifold.
rows.note: The paper says the radial-variation result is similar to that for ReLU SAEs.
rows.check: Same as R3 for JumpReLU SAEs; SAE behaviour on imposed manifolds.

rows.subject: gemma-scope-2b-pt-res layer_12
rows.operation_detail: Measured decoder-vector cosine similarity to each vector's nearest neighbor.
rows.measure: Distribution of decoder nearest-neighbor cosine similarities
rows.baseline: Random decoder vectors would be approximately orthogonal.
rows.value: The distribution is substantially skewed toward higher cosine similarities than the random-vector expectation, but the authors do not observe a very large fraction of latents with extremely high nearest-neighbor similarity.
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative summary across the displayed SAEs; individual distribution values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Decoder nearest-neighbour cosine distribution in Gemma Scope SAEs, used as a proxy for manifold tiling. It does not measure feature dimensionality or SAE completeness. The random-orthogonal baseline is only qualitative.

rows.subject: gemma-scope-2b-pt-res layer_12
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the high-cosine nearest-neighbor latents in one SAE.
rows.measure: Number and status of latents with nearest-neighbor cosine similarity > 0.97
rows.value: Between 10 and 100 latents had nearest-neighbor cosine similarity > 0.97; for each, the nearest neighbor was dead across the dataset.
rows.note: The authors infer these are not latents being used to sparsely reconstruct points on a manifold; they suggest a training artifact instead.
rows.check: 10-100 latents with cosine >0.97 whose nearest neighbours were dead. The authors call this a training artifact, not tiling. Not a measure of any version.

rows.subject: ReLU L1 SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured decoder latent nearest-neighbor cosine similarities.
rows.measure: Distribution of pairwise decoder cosine similarities
rows.value: A meaningful fraction of SAE latents have very high cosine similarity with their nearest neighbor.
rows.note: The authors note that duplicated latents could explain this result and are not strongly disincentivized by the L1 loss.

relation.reason: Section 2.1 explicitly assumes sparse multidimensional linear representations. The experiments investigate SAE behavior under those assumptions rather than establishing superposition or real feature dimensionality.

tranche.reason: Uses an assumed sparse feature representation and imposed feature manifolds to study SAE scaling and decoder geometry; these results do not directly test any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Real-model measurements concern SAE decoder geometry, with dead-neighbor and duplication caveats. The authors leave pathological scaling in real SAEs unresolved; synthetic radial variation produces early loss plateaus.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: SAE scaling depends on manifold geometry: higher-dimensional unit hyperspheres can keep accommodating latents, while radial-variation manifolds plateau near 2d_i latents (R1–R4). This tests SAE behavior on manifolds, not the dimensionality of features in real networks.
